title: Some data-driven optimism: yes, there has been a more games published on Steam recently because of AI, but more games are reaching 1000 sales
author: randomstate42
selftext:
About a year ago I published an analysis about the impact of AI disclosures on sales, which for months went largely unnoticed. Then one day after coming back from holiday I was shocked to find it was picked up by PC Gamer, Dualshockers, and even featured on Bellular News O\_o

It has been a long time since I looked at this topic and honestly, it is because it is so polarizing and I don't want to get caught up in the doom-cycle unless I feel I can genuinely contribute something useful.

But since going full-time on our business and taking a moment to really look at the data, I feel like there are some positive and helpful stories I can tell. The first is in our most recent blog post that I would like to share:  [https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-1](https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-1)

This is the first of three blogs I'm writing on the subject of AI on Steam and the message is simple. Yes, there has been A LOT of games published on Steam this year, and the amount with AI disclosures has exploded. But that has not impacted the proportion of games that went on to make at least 1000 sales (a modest and realistic target for indie developers I believe).

More competition ≠ a fixed number of winners. I think it is more complicated than that. I've just finished reading Morgan Housel's Same as Ever and I think the advice in that book applies here: the world changes but people stay more or less the same. And in reality, economies (including the gaming economy) are just a function of groups of people.

I by no means wish to minimize the impact of the changes happening right now, or down-play the pain a lot of people are feeling (my wife was laid off and I've seen my own career change dramatically, so I know what all this uncertainty feels like first hand).

But I am also tired of people screaming the sky is falling. I would like to contribute to a more nuanced discussion in the only way I know how and that is by looking at the data and asking "What is really happening? What can I control in my own world? What is the optimistic viewpoint? What next step helps move me forward?"

So I hope you enjoy the insights and I'll come back and post when part 2 is ready!

comments.author: niloony
comments.body:
The personal calendar update probably plays a significant role in this. It'd be interesting to see if the 10k+ unit sales group starts to be pulled down. As that's the bare minimum to do this full-time in wealthier countries.

Steam's algo would protect the 100k+ group. But then AI might pull down prices.

replies.author: randomstate42
replies.body:
Very good point. I do have plans to look into the impact of the personal calendar update at some point, but I was going to wait for the store changes coming in early 2027. The ground is moving fast. It is exciting to see Steam thinking seriously about indie discoverability.

As for AI pulling down prices my guess would be that this would be balanced with reduced production costs? But then if the market shifts to expecting a higher standard that effect will normalise over time? I don't know is my honest answer.

comments.author: Janupur
comments.body:
I would like to see them make a new category on steam for smaller games. Right now it's by genre but there's no sorting by the size of the game. 

I think examples of this would be Stanley's parable as an example that that's a relatively small game. This would be a great way of promoting more games because these games can be cheap and easier to make but still enjoyable. 

It's a bit hard that they expect this type of content to compete with massive 40 hour plus games

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body: This makes me wonder if on average Ai homebrew games are cheaper. Like I waited for ages for the price to drop in Atelier Yumia and it just fell to thirty bucks, but, instead, I saw a game called Beyond Galaxyland for five dollars and snatched it up right away. Same with Rangers in the South. Ai or not, looks cool, five bucks, buy. Not on sale, Atelier Yumia runs 59.99 for the base edition and 109.99 for the premium. I played the demo and enjoyed it but, a hundred ten bucks?? Hard pass.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body: 1k sales is not enough. If you pocket 10 dollars after steaks cut that is only 10k. That is like a month of pay for a game dev. And most games take months or years of effort. Top games hundreds of years.
